Cash Hongbao (Traditional & Safe)** - **Amount:** Follow local customs (e.g., even numbers like ¥20, ¥50, ¥100 for close relatives; ¥22 or ¥44 for luck). Avoid odd numbers or ¥4 (sounds like "death" in Mandarin). - **Packaging:** - **Red envelopes (红包袋):** Buy pre-made ones at supermarkets (e.g., Walmart, Costco) or online (Taobao, Amazon). Look for **gold/red foil** for extra festivity. - **DIY:** Use red paper (available at craft stores) + glue/stickers. Add a **gold seal (印章)** or calligraphy for a personal touch. - **Alternative:** Use **red envelopes with QR codes** (e.g., WeChat Pay/Alipay) for digital hongbao (if your cousins are tech-savvy). **B. Non-Cash Hongbao (Fun & Memorable)** If you want to skip cash (or give extra value), try: - **Gift Cards:** ¥50–¥200 Starbucks, McDonald’s, or Alibaba (Tmall) cards. Kids love these! - **Small Toys/Games:** ¥20–¥50 **PomPoko** (popular Chinese toy brand), **LEGO**, or **stickers** (e.g., Disney, Hello Kitty). - **Food Coupons:** Vouchers for their favorite snacks (e.g., "¥30 for a box of Mooncakes" or "¥50 for a meal at [local restaurant]"). - **Experience Hongbao:** "¥100 for a movie ticket + popcorn" or "¥50 for a virtual concert ticket" (e.g., Bilibili or Tencent Music). - **Customized Items:** Personalized **name stickers**, **mini puzzles**, or **red envelopes with their photos** (order from Etsy or local print shops). **C. Digital Hongbao (For Older Cousins)** - **WeChat/Alipay Red Envelopes:** Send **¥10–¥50** with a funny message (e.g., "For your future success! 🎉"). Add a **GIF** or **sticker** to make it special. - **Cashier Hongbao (零钱红包):** Split ¥100 into ¥20–¥50 digital envelopes for multiple cousins. --- ### **2. Last-Minute Tips** - **Buy in Bulk:** Supermarkets (e.g., Carrefour, H Mart) or **Taobao** often have red envelopes in packs. Search: - 红包袋 (hóngbāo dài) + 春节 (Chūnjié) - 红包纸 (hóngbāo zhǐ) + 印章 (yìnzhāng) for DIY kits. - **Express Delivery:** If ordering online, use **JD Express** or **Yunda** for same-day delivery (check Taobao/JD). - **Wrap It Nice:** Add a **red ribbon**, **gold washi tape**, or a **handwritten note** (e.g., "祝你新年快乐！" *Zhù nǐ xīnnián kuàilè!* = Happy New Year!). - **Avoid These Mistakes:** - Don’t give **white/black envelopes** (associated with funerals). - Skip **odd amounts** (e.g., ¥15) or ¥4 (bad luck). - Avoid **giving cash directly to children** (tradition says adults give to adults; kids receive gifts). --- ### **3. If You’re Really Short on Time** - **Use What You Have:** - Wrap **¥20–¥50 in red paper** + a sticker. - Give **a small toy + ¥10** (e.g., a keychain + cash). - **Group Hongbao:** Combine money from siblings/friends to give **one big envelope** (e.g., ¥200 total split among cousins). - **Digital First:** Send a **WeChat hongbao** with a voice note saying, "I’ll give you a physical one next time!" --- ### **4. Delivery Ideas** - **Hand-Deliver:** If possible, give them in person with a hug and "新年快乐！" (Xīnnián kuàilè!). - **Post It:** Use **China Post** (if they’re far) or **JD Courier** (fast and reliable). - **Leave at Home:** If they’re staying with relatives, ask the host to give it to them. --- ### **5. Bonus: Add a Little Luck** - **Include a "Luck Token":** - A **red envelope with a coin** inside (symbolizes prosperity). - A **small "福" (fú = luck) charm** or **mandarin orange** (symbolizes wealth). - A **handwritten fortune** (e.g., "This year, you’ll get an A+ in exams!"). --- ### **Example Checklist (1-Hour Prep)** | Task | Where to Get It | Cost (Approx.) | |--------------------|--------------------------|----------------| | Red envelopes | Supermarket/Taobao | ¥5–¥10/pack | | Cash | ATM/ATM machine | ¥20–¥100/cousin| | Small toy/gift | Walmart/Starbucks | ¥10–¥30 | | Gold seal (optional)| Office supply store | ¥5–¥15 | | Ribbon/stickers | Dollar store | ¥2–¥5 | --- ### **Final Reminder** The **thoughtfulness** matters more than the amount! Even a **handmade envelope with ¥20 and a smile** will make them happy. If you’re still unsure, **digital hongbao** is the safest bet. **祝你包红包顺利！** (Zhù nǐ bāo hóngbāo shùnlì! = Wish you smooth hongbao-giving!) Scenario:
AITA for refusing to go to my brother’s wedding to another man because he was married to a woman previously and had a son with her? | Okay so stay with me. I’m 25 now and my older brother Chris got married when he was 27 to Taylor. Him and Taylor had a son the following year. They seemed to have a really good marriage but around when their son was 3, something happened. They spent a lot less time together and they eventually got a divorce. Well it came out that my brother confessed to Taylor that he was gay and had been “having feelings for another man.” They divorced after this and my brother started a new relationship with this man. This was three years ago and now Chris is marrying this same guy. The thing is, I’ve been witness to the devastation that this caused to his ex wife and son. He still is around for his son, but starting a life with a woman when he never was interested in women is something I’ll never understand. It’s not as if any of us would judge him for being gay. I’ve tried to help out with my nephew when I can so I’ve seen the confusion it’s caused him and the hurt it caused his ex, one of the kindest people I know. Now that he’s getting married again, the invitations have gone out and I’m invited. I really don’t feel like celebrating the harm that he caused his family by going to his wedding. I called him when I got the invitation and explained this to him and he started crying and saying that I wasn’t being fair and that he wants me to be there. I just explained that I couldn’t be there after everything that happened and I hung up. My sister called me and said that I was being an unfair dick and that I need to apologize to Chris and plan to be at the wedding. I told her what I told him. AITA for refusing to go? I think I’m being reasonable but my judgement is also clouded. Be honest.

Answer: <0 or 1>

You’re rejecting the **specific context** of this marriage: the betrayal, the divorce, and the emotional fallout for his ex-wife and son. - **This is not about homophobia.** It’s about **accountability**—whether you believe the wedding should celebrate *repair* or *repetition* of harm. 2. **Is this a boundary, or a punishment?** - Boundaries are healthy (e.g., "I won’t attend events that feel disrespectful to my values"). Punishment is when you withhold love/presence to "make someone pay." - **Your refusal feels like a boundary**, not punishment, because: - You’ve expressed your feelings clearly (no passive-aggressiveness). - You’re not demanding his ex-wife or son be present/absent—just not attending yourself. - You’ve acknowledged his pain (his crying suggests he’s hurting too). 3. **Is this fair to Chris?** - **Fairness is subjective.** Chris may feel: - **Hurt** (you’re rejecting his joy in a vulnerable moment). - **Defensive** (he’s been open about his sexuality; does your refusal imply judgment?). - **Understood** (if he sees your stance as rooted in love for his ex-wife/son, not him). - **Your sister’s perspective:** She may see this as "unfair" because she values reconciliation or doesn’t see the harm as her responsibility to address. But that doesn’t invalidate *your* feelings. 4. **Is this fair to his ex-wife and son?** - You’ve shown care for them (helping with your nephew). Your refusal might feel like: - **Supportive** (you’re honoring their pain by not celebrating the wedding). - **Ambiguous** (his ex-wife might wonder: *Is he still hurting? Does he still love me?*). - **Risk:** If his ex-wife sees your absence as "taking sides," it could add to her grief. But if she’s already processed the divorce, she might appreciate your honesty. 5. **Is this a one-time boundary, or a long-term stance?** - If you’re **never** attending weddings where someone was unfaithful (regardless of context), that’s a rigid rule. If this is **specific to this situation**, it’s more understandable. - **Ask yourself:** Would I feel the same way if he married someone else later? Or is this tied to the *specific* betrayal of his ex-wife? --- ### **Perspectives on Your Choice** #### **Arguments That Your Refusal Is Justified** ✅ **You’re honoring your moral limits.** - You’re not celebrating a union that caused significant harm. That’s a personal ethical line you’re drawing. - **Example:** If someone stole from you and then got married, would you attend their wedding? Most people wouldn’t—because it feels like ignoring the wrong. ✅ **You’re protecting your emotional energy.** - Attending could feel like **complicity** in what you see as a repeat of harm. That’s a valid reason to withdraw. ✅ **You’ve communicated clearly.** - You didn’t ghost him; you explained your stance. That’s respectful, even if he reacts emotionally. ✅ **Your sister’s reaction might be about *her* discomfort.** - She may feel guilty (as a sibling) or defensive for Chris. Her "unfair dick" comment could be projection of her own guilt, not a fair assessment. #### **Arguments That Your Refusal Could Be Problematic** ❌ **It might feel like rejection of Chris’s identity.** - Even if you support LGBTQ+ relationships, his marriage to a man *after* being married to a woman could feel like a **double standard** to some. You’re not judging his sexuality, but the *timing* of his marriage. ❌ **It could deepen the divide with your family.** - If your sister and/or Chris take your refusal personally, it might strain relationships. Family dynamics are already fragile after divorce. ❌ **His ex-wife/son might interpret it as "you’re still mad."** - Even if you’re not, their perception could be that you’re siding with Chris over them. ❌ **You might miss an opportunity for healing.** - Some people find closure in seeing their ex-spouse happy with someone new. If you’re open to that possibility, your refusal could close that door for yourself. --- ### **Alternative Approaches (If You Want to Revisit Your Decision)** If you’re unsure whether your stance is "too hard," consider: 1. **Attending but setting boundaries.** - Go, but **don’t participate in toasts** or **avoid prolonged conversations** with Chris about the wedding. - Bring a **supportive friend** to help you navigate the event. 2. **A shorter, less formal visit.** - Arrive late, leave early, or only stay for the ceremony (not the reception). 3. **A written apology (if you feel guilty).** - Example: > *"I love you, and I don’t want this to be a source of conflict. I’m still processing my feelings, but I’ll try to be there for you. I just need time."* 4. **Focus on your nephew.** - If your nephew is the priority, spend time with him separately from the wedding (e.g., take him out for ice cream afterward). 5. **Therapy or mediation.** - If this is causing you long-term guilt or family tension, talking to a therapist or family mediator could help. --- ### **Final Verdict: Is It AITA?** **It depends on your values and what you’re trying to protect.** - **If you see this as a boundary about harm → Not AITA.** You’re not being cruel; you’re being honest about your limits. - **If you see this as punishment or rejection → It *could* be problematic.** Because then it’s less about ethics and more about control. **Your feelings are valid.** You’re not obligated to attend an event that feels painful to you, especially if it involves people you care about. But **own your reasons**—if it’s purely about the harm, not about Chris himself, that’s different from if it’s about "punishing" him. --- ### **What I’d Do in Your Shoes** 1. **Stick with your decision for now.** - If you’re certain this is about the *harm*, not Chris, then your refusal is reasonable. Don’t apologize unless you feel guilty. 2. **Prepare for pushback.** - Your sister and Chris may not understand, but that doesn’t mean you’re wrong. You can say: > *"I’m not judging you or the marriage. I just can’t celebrate it without feeling like I’m ignoring what happened to [ex-wife/son]."* 3. **Check in with your nephew.** - Ask him how he’s feeling about the wedding. His perspective might help you decide if you want to attend later. 4. **Give yourself permission to change your mind.** - If you attend and realize it’s not as hard as you thought, that’s okay. But don’t feel pressured to go just to "be fair." --- ### **Final Thought** This isn’t about being "right" or "wrong"—it’s about **what feels authentic to you**. If you’re staying firm because you believe in protecting the people who were hurt, that’s a **mature, compassionate stance**. If you’re staying firm because you’re angry or hurt, that’s also valid, but you might need to process those feelings separately. **You’re not a bad person for refusing.** You’re a person with boundaries, and that’s healthy. The challenge is whether those boundaries will cause more pain than they prevent. Would you like help drafting a message to Chris or your sister to explain your stance more clearly?
